record.context_brief: Formal framework and virtual scientist direction
record.original_question: How can a formal active representation learning framework support intelligent model building from sequential, incomplete observations, learn the latent structure of an object or phenomenon, reuse structural similarities across related problems, and ultimately enable virtual scientist agents that curiously explore complex processes and discover or exploit their symmetries?

evidence.quote: Active Representation Learning highlights the need for a framework capable of capturing model building through sequential, incomplete observations, and the need to learn the underlying structure of a latent object or phenomenon.

Ideally, the intelligent agent can learn structural similarities across a larger class of similar problems and use this information the next time a similarly structured problem is encountered, e.g. when a similar specimen is examined under the microscope.

Ideally, the community would work towards and eventually achieve a virtual scientist framework that allows us to build agents that can curiously explore complex processes the way humans do, potentially discovering and exploiting its symmetries.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a formal mathematical framework for active representation learning with the following requirements. Consider an unknown latent object or phenomenon X belonging to some class of structured objects (e.g., equipped with group actions, symmetries, or hierarchical decompositions). An agent interacts with X by sequentially choosing queries q_1, q_2, ... from a query space Q according to a policy π, and receives partial, possibly noisy observations o_t = O(X, q_t) ∈ Y. After T rounds, the agent outputs a representation R_T ∈ R of X.

Design and analyze such a framework so that it simultaneously achieves the following objectives:

1. (Sequential model building from incomplete observations.) Define a notion of representation quality L(R_T, X) and provide sample-complexity / regret guarantees on the number of queries T needed to recover R_T with L(R_T, X) ≤ ε for a given ε > 0, when only partial observations of X are available at each step.

2. (Latent structure recovery.) Provide a precise definition of the "latent structure" of X (e.g., as a generative model, a graphical model, a group-theoretic invariant, or a category-theoretic object) and prove that the framework recovers this latent structure under stated identifiability assumptions.

3. (Transfer across related problems.) Formalize a class C of related problems sharing structural similarities (for example, problems related by a group action, a fibration over a common base, or a shared latent variable model). Prove that representations learned on one X ∈ C can be reused to reduce the query complexity for learning a new X' ∈ C, and quantify the achievable speed-up.

4. (Symmetry discovery and exploitation.) Formalize a notion of symmetry of X as a group G acting on the observation/query spaces that leaves the conditional distribution of observations invariant. Provide an algorithm within the framework that, with high probability, identifies a generating set of G from sequential observations, and show that exploiting G strictly reduces the query complexity in objective (1).

State and prove the existence (or impossibility) of an algorithmic instantiation of the framework that simultaneously satisfies (1)–(4) for a nontrivial class of latent objects.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction calling for the development of a formal active representation learning framework that combines sequential querying, latent structure recovery, transfer across related tasks, and symmetry discovery. No known work simultaneously addresses all four desiderata in a unified formal framework; the problem appears to remain open as of 2026.
